title: H-1B Extensions Now Carry $4,000 Biometric Fee as New US Rule Takes Effect
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security has expanded the 9/11 biometric entry-exit fee to cover same-employer H-1B and L-1 extensions, raising recurring immigration costs for visa-dependent employers.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security's final rule, effective September 9, 2026, requires "covered employers" to pay the $4,000 H-1B or $4,500 L-1 biometric fee on every extension-of-status petition — including same-employer renewals that were previously exempt.
  • A covered employer has at least 50 US employees, more than half of whom hold H-1B or L-1 status. The fee is paid by the employer; workers cannot be asked to foot it.
  • DHS concedes its earlier reading of the 2015 law was wrong, saying Congress intended the fee to apply to all extension petitions. The share of covered employers' H-1B petitions attracting the fee could jump from about 27% to roughly 75%.
  • The government projects $37.9 million in additional collections in fiscal 2026 and $40 million in fiscal 2027, funding the biometric entry-exit program that verifies the identity of foreign nationals entering and leaving the US.

The cost of keeping an H-1B worker in the United States has gone up. A final rule from the Department of Homeland Security, which took effect on September 9, extends the $4,000 9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee to H-1B and L-1 extension petitions filed by certain employers — even when the worker is simply continuing with the same company.

What exactly changes

Until now, the biometric fee generally applied to petitions for initial employment or a change of employer. Extensions filed by the same employer for the same worker were typically exempt if the separate fraud-prevention fee did not apply. That carve-out is gone. Under the new rule, covered employers must pay the fee on all extension-of-status petitions, regardless of whether the fraud fee applies.

https://x.com/anttsinc/status/2098037373661528322

The amounts are not new. Congress established the biometric fee in 2015. What changes is the number of petitions on which covered employers must pay it — $4,000 for each qualifying H-1B petition and $4,500 for each qualifying L-1 petition. Amended petitions that do not seek an extension of authorized status remain exempt.

Who has to pay

The fee lands only on "covered employers" — companies with at least 50 employees in the United States where more than 50% of the US workforce, counted in aggregate, holds H-1B, L-1A or L-1B status. A company with 50 or more US workers does not automatically qualify; both conditions must be met.

The financial obligation rests entirely on the employer. DHS dismissed proposals that would have let foreign professionals pay the charge themselves if their companies were unwilling, stating: "The statutes and existing regulations specify that the fee is required to be paid by the employer."

"The best interpretation of that statute is that the 9-11 Biometric Fee applies to all extension of status petitions even when the Fraud Fee is not applicable."

— US Department of Homeland Security

The scale of the expansion

The expansion is substantial. Between fiscal 2018 and 2025, about 27% of H-1B petitions submitted by covered employers attracted the biometric fee. Had the new interpretation been in effect, approximately 75% of their H-1B petitions would have been subject to it, according to the department.

DHS estimates the change will bring in an additional $37.9 million in fiscal 2026 and $40 million in fiscal 2027, funding the biometric entry-exit program that verifies the identity of foreign nationals entering and leaving the US.

Background: a correction, not a new tax

DHS is framing the rule as a statutory correction rather than a policy invention. The department says its earlier interpretation of the law had been incorrect: when Congress created the fee in 2015, it included applications for extensions, but DHS had linked collection to circumstances in which the fraud-prevention fee also applied.

"The regulatory changes correct DHS's interpretation of statutory language to require that covered employers submit the 9-11 Biometric Fee for all extension of status petitions," the department said. The new requirement applies prospectively — it will not be imposed retroactively on past or pending petitions.

What it means for Indian workers

The shift falls heaviest on large technology and IT-services firms — the heaviest users of the H-1B program — and on Indian professionals, who dominate the category. USCIS data show about 72% of H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025 were for continuing employment, and Indians accounted for roughly 77.6% of those renewals.

The department acknowledged warnings that higher recurring costs could discourage companies from retaining H-1B workers and disadvantage those in lengthy green-card queues, but rejected the concerns — calling the fee small relative to wages and hiring costs and saying it expects no reduction in overall H-1B hiring.

What's next

Employers must now factor the fee into every extension filing. Watch for industry pushback: a similar 2020 attempt to extend the fee to renewals was blocked in court, and employers say the cumulative cost of the administration's H-1B fee stack is reshaping sponsorship decisions.

nri_angle: Indians receive the majority of H-1B visas and renewals, so professionals at visa-dependent employers face the most indirect exposure if firms cut back on extensions because of the recurring cost.
